slides.heading: The Flower
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the reproductive organ of a flowering plant and the whorls it is built from.

nodes.label: Four whorls: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium

visual.alt: Flow from the pedicel to the thalamus to the four whorls of a flower

slides.narration: A flower is a shoot that has become specialised for reproduction. It stands on a stalk, and the tip of the stalk carries four rings of parts, called whorls, one inside another.

slides.heading: A bisexual flower
slides.body_md: A **bisexual flower** has both **stamens** (male) and a **pistil** (female) in the same flower.

slides.narration: Here is a flower cut lengthways. Outside are the green sepals and the coloured petals. Inside are the stamens, each with an anther on a filament, and in the centre the pistil with its stigma, style and ovary.

slides.heading: Parts of the flower

rows: The stalk that holds the flower
The swollen tip of the pedicel that carries all the whorls
The outermost whorl: sepals, usually green
The next whorl: petals, usually coloured
The male whorl: all the stamens
The female whorl: the pistil, made of carpels

visual.alt: Table of the pedicel, thalamus, calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium

slides.narration: Learn the order from outside to inside: calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium. All of them sit on the thalamus, which is the swollen tip of the flower stalk, called the pedicel.

slides.heading: Quick check: the swollen tip
slides.body_md: Which part of a flower carries all the whorls?
slides.narration: It is the swollen tip of the stalk.

slides.heading: The four whorls
slides.body_md: The **calyx** and **corolla** are the **non-essential** whorls; the **androecium** and **gynoecium** are the **essential** whorls.

visual.alt: The four whorls of a flower seen from above

slides.narration: Seen from above, the whorls form rings. The outer two protect the flower and attract insects, but the flower can still reproduce without them. The inner two, the stamens and the pistil, are the essential parts.

slides.heading: Complete and incomplete flowers

rows: Has all four whorls: calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium
Lacks one or more of the four whorls
Has both stamens and a pistil
Has only stamens or only a pistil
Male or female flower of papaya

visual.alt: Table of complete, incomplete, bisexual and unisexual flowers with meaning and example

slides.narration: A complete flower has all four whorls. Anything less is incomplete. Bisexual and unisexual describe the essential whorls only. So a wheat flower is bisexual but incomplete, because it has no showy sepals or petals.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classifying flowers
slides.body_md: Flower X has sepals, petals, stamens and a pistil. Flower Y has stamens only. Flower Z has stamens and a pistil but no petals. Classify each.
bullets: Step 1: count the **whorls**. X has **four**, Y has **one**, Z has **three** (calyx may be absent too).
Step 2: all four means **complete**; fewer means **incomplete**.
Step 3: check the essential whorls: X and Z have **both**, so are **bisexual**; Y has only stamens, so is **unisexual**.

visual.alt: Worked table classifying flowers X, Y and Z as complete or incomplete and bisexual or unisexual

slides.narration: First count the whorls. All four makes a flower complete. Then look at the stamens and the pistil. Both present means bisexual, only one means unisexual. So flower Z is incomplete but bisexual.

slides.heading: Quick check: a complete flower
slides.body_md: A flower is called complete when it has
slides.narration: Count the whorls.

slides.heading: Roles of sepals and petals

rows: Protects the flower bud; makes food by photosynthesis; later supports the opened flower
Attracts insects for pollination; may have scent and nectar; protects stamens and pistil

visual.alt: Table of the roles of the calyx and the corolla

slides.narration: Sepals are like a green cover that protects the bud. Petals are the advertisement. Their colour and scent draw insects to the flower, which helps carry pollen from flower to flower.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting parts
slides.body_md: A flower has 5 sepals, 5 petals, 10 stamens and 1 pistil. How many parts does it have, and how many are essential?
bullets: Step 2: non-essential = sepals and petals = 5 + 5 = **10**.
Step 3: essential = stamens and pistil = 10 + 1 = **11**.

visual.alt: Worked table: ten non-essential parts, eleven essential parts and twenty-one parts in all

slides.narration: Sort the parts into the two groups first. Sepals and petals are the non-essential ones. Stamens and the pistil are the essential ones. Then add the groups to find the total number of parts.

slides.heading: Quick check: the coloured whorl
slides.body_md: Which whorl attracts insects to a flower?
slides.narration: Think of the bright part.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Pedicel, thalamus, calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium.
Bisexual: stamens and pistil together. Complete: all four whorls.
Calyx protects; corolla attracts.
Androecium and gynoecium are the essential whorls.

visual.alt: Summary table of the four whorls, what each is made of and its job

slides.narration: To recap. A flower has four whorls on the thalamus. The calyx protects, the corolla attracts, the androecium makes pollen and the gynoecium holds the ovules. A complete flower has all four.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: A **complete** flower has all **four whorls**; **bisexual** only refers to stamens and pistil.
Write the whorls from **outside to inside**.
In a diagram show the **thalamus** and **pedicel** too.
Label with **ruled lines** that touch the part.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Do not mix up complete and bisexual. Complete means all four whorls, bisexual means both stamens and pistil. Name the whorls from outside to inside, include the thalamus in your drawing, and label with ruled lines.

decks.title: The Flower — Part 2: Stamen, pistil, inflorescence and placentation
goals: State the parts of the stamen and the pistil and their functions
Explain why the androecium and gynoecium are essential

slides.heading: Stamen, Pistil and Arrangement
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the male and female organs, and how flowers and ovules are arranged.

visual.alt: Flow from the flower to the stamen that makes pollen and the pistil that holds ovules

slides.narration: The stamens and the pistil are the parts that actually make new seeds. After studying them we look at two ideas about arrangement: how flowers are grouped, and how ovules sit inside the ovary.

slides.heading: Stamen and pistil
slides.body_md: A **stamen** has an **anther** and a **filament**. A **pistil** has a **stigma**, a **style** and an **ovary** with **ovules**.

visual.alt: A stamen and a pistil with their parts labelled

slides.narration: The anther at the top of the stamen makes the pollen grains, and the filament holds it up. In the pistil, the sticky stigma catches pollen, the style carries it down, and the ovary holds the ovules.

slides.heading: Functions of the parts

rows: Makes and holds pollen grains in pollen sacs
Holds the anther up so that pollen can be carried away
Sticky top that receives pollen grains
Stalk joining the stigma to the ovary
Swollen base that contains the ovules

visual.alt: Table of anther, filament, stigma, style and ovary with the whorl and function of each

slides.narration: Each part has one clear job. Anthers make pollen, filaments hold anthers up, stigmas catch pollen, styles connect, and the ovary protects the ovules inside it.

slides.heading: Quick check: the stamen
slides.body_md: Which two parts make up a stamen?
slides.narration: Think of the male whorl.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting pollen
slides.body_md: A flower has 6 stamens. Each anther has 4 pollen sacs, and each sac holds 300 pollen grains. How many pollen grains does the flower make?
bullets: Step 1: grains in one anther = 4 × 300 = **1200**.
Step 2: grains in the flower = 6 × 1200 = **7200**.

visual.alt: Worked table: one thousand two hundred grains per anther, six stamens and seven thousand two hundred grains in the flower

slides.narration: Work from the smallest unit. Multiply the number of pollen sacs by the grains in each sac to get the grains in one anther. Then multiply by the number of stamens to get the total for the flower.

slides.heading: Quick check: the pistil
slides.body_md: Which part of the pistil receives the pollen grains?
slides.narration: It is sticky.

slides.heading: Essential and non-essential whorls

rows: Protect and attract, but seeds can form without them
Make the gametes and the seeds; without them no seeds form

visual.alt: Table of the essential and non-essential whorls with reasons

slides.narration: The outer whorls help but are not necessary for making seeds. The stamens make the male gametes, and the pistil holds the ovules with the female gametes. So these two are called the essential whorls.

slides.body_md: An **inflorescence** is a group of flowers borne together on one **flowering axis**.

sections.heading: 1. Structure of a bisexual flower; complete and incomplete flowers
sections.body_md:
A **flower** is the reproductive organ of a flowering plant. It stands on a stalk, the **pedicel**, whose swollen tip is the **thalamus** (receptacle). The thalamus carries four **whorls**, from outside to inside:
1. **Calyx**: the sepals (usually green).
2. **Corolla**: the petals (usually coloured).
3. **Androecium**: the stamens (male).
4. **Gynoecium** (pistil): the carpels (female).

A **bisexual flower** has both stamens and pistil (Hibiscus); a **unisexual flower** has only one of them (papaya has male and female flowers on different plants).

| Kind | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Complete** | All four whorls present | Hibiscus |
| **Incomplete** | One or more whorls missing | Wheat (no showy sepals or petals); male flower of papaya |

A complete flower is always bisexual. A bisexual flower may be incomplete.

**Diagram:** draw the flower in long section: pedicel, thalamus, sepal, petal, stamen (filament, anther), pistil (stigma, style, ovary, ovule).

sections.heading: 2. Essential and non-essential whorls
sections.body_md:
**Non-essential (accessory) whorls**
- **Calyx (sepals):** green; **protect** the bud; can make food by photosynthesis; support the opened flower.
- **Corolla (petals):** coloured, often scented, with nectar; **attract insects** for pollination; protect the stamens and the pistil.

**Essential whorls** (needed to form seeds)
- **Androecium:** a number of **stamens**. Each stamen has an **anther** (usually two lobes with pollen sacs that make and hold **pollen grains**) and a **filament** that holds the anther.
- **Gynoecium (pistil):** one or more **carpels**; each has a **stigma** (sticky top that **receives pollen**), a **style** (stalk joining stigma and ovary) and an **ovary** (swollen base containing **ovules**, each holding an egg cell). After fertilisation ovules develop into seeds.

The sticky part of the pistil that receives pollen.

sections.heading: 3. Inflorescence and placentation (meaning only)
sections.body_md:
**Inflorescence** is the arrangement of a group of flowers on a **flowering axis** (the main stalk is the **peduncle**; each flower has its own pedicel). Small flowers grouped in an inflorescence are more conspicuous to insects and wind. The **types of inflorescence** are not required in this course.

**Placentation** is the **arrangement of the ovules on the placenta inside the ovary**. The **placenta** is the cushion of tissue on the ovary wall to which the ovules are attached. The **types of placentation** are not required; the meaning alone is asked.

key_terms.definition_md: A group of flowers borne together on one flowering axis.
Tissue of the ovary wall to which the ovules are attached.
The arrangement of ovules in the ovary.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up **complete** (all four whorls) and **bisexual** (stamens and pistil together).
- Writing the ovary or the pistil as the whole of the female whorl without naming the **gynoecium**.
- Giving only the colour as the role of petals, without **attracting insects**.
- Drawing the stigma below the ovary, or leaving out the **thalamus** and **pedicel**.
- Writing types of inflorescence or placentation: only the **meaning** is required.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, a part, an odd one out **with its category**.
- 2 marks: two functions or two differences matched point for point.
- 3 marks: a neat, labelled diagram (outline of the parts, key features, correct labels).
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation or diagram with parts of 3, 3 and 4 marks; one part is usually a labelled diagram.

questions.stem_md: Which part of a flower carries all the whorls?
questions.solution_md: The swollen tip of the pedicel, the thalamus, carries the whorls — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A flower is called complete when it has
questions.solution_md: A complete flower has all four whorls — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which whorl attracts insects to a flower?
questions.solution_md: Brightly coloured petals draw insects — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which two parts make up a stamen?
questions.solution_md: A stamen is an anther on a filament — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which part of the pistil receives the pollen grains?
questions.solution_md: The sticky stigma receives pollen — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A group of flowers borne together on one flowering axis is called
questions.solution_md: A group of flowers on a flowering axis is an inflorescence — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The arrangement of ovules inside the ovary is called
questions.solution_md: Placentation is the arrangement of ovules on the placenta — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student finds a flower with five green sepals, five red petals, many stamens and one pistil. The flower is
questions.solution_md: All four whorls are present, so it is complete; it has both stamens and a pistil, so it is bisexual — option (b).

questions.stem_md: On a papaya tree the flowers have petals and stamens but no pistil. These flowers are
questions.solution_md: The gynoecium is missing, so the flower is incomplete, and it has only stamens, so it is unisexual — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A wheat flower has stamens and a pistil but no showy sepals or petals. It is
questions.solution_md: It has both essential whorls, so it is bisexual, but two whorls are missing, so it is incomplete — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the figure of a flower, which letter marks the part that receives the pollen grains?
questions.solution_md: C is the stigma; A is a petal, B an anther, D the ovary and E a sepal — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
In a practical class a student pulls apart a Hibiscus flower and finds, from outside to inside, green leaf-like parts, large bright petals, a tube of stamens and a pistil with a sticky top.

(a) State whether the flower is complete or incomplete, and bisexual or unisexual. Give a reason for each. [2]

(b) Name the outer two whorls and state one function of each. [3]

(c) Name the parts of the pistil and state the function of the stigma. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the flower in long section, naming six parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Complete**, because all four whorls (calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium) are present; **bisexual**, because it has both stamens and a pistil.

**(b)** **Calyx** (green sepals): **protects** the bud. **Corolla** (bright petals): **attracts insects**. (Both whorls named and one function each.)

**(c)** **Stigma, style and ovary**. The stigma is **sticky** and **receives the pollen grains**.

**(d)** A **pedicel** and **thalamus**, **sepals**, **petals**, **stamens** (anther and filament) and a **pistil** (stigma, style, ovary). Six labels with ruled lines.

questions.solution_md: Complete and bisexual; calyx protects, corolla attracts; stigma, style, ovary; labelled flower.

questions.stem_md:
A farmer has a papaya orchard. The flowers of some trees have 5 stamens and no pistil; the flowers of other trees have a pistil and no stamens. Each anther of a male flower has 4 pollen sacs, each holding 250 pollen grains.

(a) Classify each kind of flower as complete or incomplete and as bisexual or unisexual. [3]

(b) Name the whorl present only in the female tree and the whorl present only in the male tree. [2]

(c) Calculate the number of pollen grains made by one male flower. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a stamen. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Both kinds are **incomplete** and **unisexual**: the male flower has no gynoecium, the female flower has no androecium (and neither is bisexual).

**(b)** Female tree: **gynoecium** (pistil). Male tree: **androecium** (stamens).

**(c)** Grains per anther = 4 × 250 = 1000; per flower = 5 × 1000 = **5000**.

**(d)** A **filament** with a two-lobed **anther** showing **pollen sacs** with pollen grains. Three labels.

questions.solution_md: Incomplete and unisexual; gynoecium and androecium; 5000 grains; labelled stamen.

questions.stem_md:
A student examines a flower of wheat under a hand lens. She sees stamens with dangling anthers and a pistil with a feathery stigma, but no bright petals and no green sepals.

(a) Is this flower complete? Is it bisexual? Give reasons. [2]

(b) Name the essential whorls of a flower and state why they are essential. [2]

(c) Suggest why a flower without bright petals may still form seeds. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the pistil, naming the stigma, style, ovary and ovule. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Not complete**: the calyx and corolla are missing. It is **bisexual**: it has both stamens and a pistil.

**(b)** The **androecium** and the **gynoecium**. They are essential because the androecium makes **pollen** and the gynoecium holds the **ovules**; **seeds cannot form without them**.

**(c)** Bright petals only **attract insects**. Seeds form from the **stamens and the pistil**, so the flower can still make seeds if pollen reaches the stigma in another way (for example carried by wind).

**(d)** A **stigma** on top of a **style**, joined to an **ovary** that contains one or more **ovules**. Four labels.

questions.solution_md: Incomplete but bisexual; androecium and gynoecium make gametes; petals only attract; labelled pistil.

marking_scheme.step: Seeds depend on stamens and pistil

questions.stem_md:
A mango branch carries one flowering stalk with 120 small flowers. A farmer finds that only 15 percent of them set fruit.

(a) Define inflorescence. [2]

(b) Calculate how many flowers set fruit and how many do not. [2]

(c) Define placentation. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of an ovary in long section, showing the ovules attached to the placenta. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** An **inflorescence** is a group of flowers borne together on one flowering axis, the main stalk being the peduncle.

**(b)** Fruits = 15 ÷ 100 × 120 = **18**; not setting fruit = 120 − 18 = **102**.

**(c)** **Placentation** is the **arrangement of ovules** on the placenta inside the ovary.

**(d)** An oval **ovary wall**, a **placenta** on the wall, **ovules** attached to it, and the base of the **style** above. Labels: ovary wall, placenta, ovule, style.

(a) Name the parts A and E and state one function of each. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:

**(c)** C is the **stigma** and D the **ovary**; they are joined by the **style**: the stigma receives pollen at the top, and the ovary at the base holds the ovules.

**(d)** Four **concentric rings**: **calyx** outermost, then **corolla**, then **androecium**, and the **gynoecium** at the centre. Labels.

questions.stem_md:
A nursery owner sorts four kinds of flower. P has calyx, corolla, stamens and a pistil. Q has calyx, corolla and stamens only. R has calyx, corolla and a pistil only. S has stamens and a pistil only.

(a) Classify each flower as complete or incomplete, and as bisexual or unisexual. [4]

(b) Which flowers can make pollen grains? Give a reason. [2]

(c) Explain why S is bisexual but incomplete. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the stamen of flower Q, naming two parts. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** P: **complete, bisexual**. Q: **incomplete, unisexual** (male). R: **incomplete, unisexual** (female). S: **incomplete, bisexual**.

**(b)** **P, Q and S** can make pollen grains, because they have **stamens**, and pollen is made in the anthers of the stamens.

**(c)** S has both essential whorls, so it is **bisexual**, but the **calyx and corolla** are missing, so not all four whorls are present: it is **incomplete**.

**(d)** A **filament** with an **anther** at the top; labels: filament and anther.

questions.solution_md: P complete bisexual; Q and R incomplete unisexual; S incomplete bisexual; P, Q and S make pollen grains; S lacks calyx and corolla; labelled stamen.
